profile.name: Sebastian Del Val
profile.title: Vehicle Dynamics & Performance Engineer
profile.intro: From a vehicle model to a decision at the track. I work at the intersection of simulation, controls and race performance.
profile.about:
Motorsport first drew me in through the cars, the competition and the engineering behind every fraction of a second. It became the reason I chose Mechanical Engineering, joined Formula Student and moved to the UK: to become the strongest motorsport engineer I am capable of becoming.

Across three seasons at E-Tech Racing, I worked on vehicle dynamics, simulation, controls, telemetry and setup development. I built the team’s first full-vehicle digital twin and progressed from Performance Engineer to Head of Performance in 2025–2026. Testing taught me to question assumptions, correlate models with real data and turn analysis into decisions at the track. At Montesa Honda, industrialising a robotic welding cell added a different discipline: taking responsibility for quality, cost, reliability and delivery in production.

Today, I am studying an MSc in Motorsport Engineering at Oxford Brookes University and remain involved with Oxford Brookes Racing. My focus is the relationship between car, driver, data and lap time. I want to keep learning through simulation, testing and trackside work, and become an engineer a team can rely on under pressure: technically capable, accountable and relentless about finding performance. Motorsport started as a passion. I am building it into a profession.

projects.title: Full-vehicle digital twin
projects.summary: Building the team’s first complete vehicle model, from the ground up.
projects.approach:
The development of the simulator began with the creation of a complete vehicle model in IPG CarMaker. I first established a common vehicle coordinate system and parameterised the fundamental physical characteristics of the car, including total mass, weight distribution, centre of gravity, sprung and unsprung masses and the principal moments of inertia. Particular attention was given to these parameters, as inaccuracies at this stage would directly affect load transfer, yaw response, braking behaviour and the overall dynamic response of the virtual vehicle.

Once the basic vehicle architecture had been defined, I collected engineering data from the different technical departments within the team and translated it into parameters that could be used within the simulation environment. This required bringing together information that had originally been generated for different purposes and adapting it into a consistent full-vehicle model. Suspension and cooling-system behaviour were integrated using MATLAB, Simulink and Simscape, while additional subsystem models were developed in Simulink and connected to CarMaker so that the different systems could interact with each other rather than being analysed independently.

Tyre modelling was treated as one of the most important parts of the project because virtually every vehicle-dynamics calculation depends on the forces generated at the contact patch. I implemented a Pacejka Magic Formula 6.1 model to represent the relationship between vertical load, slip angle, longitudinal slip, camber and the resulting longitudinal and lateral forces. This allowed the model to reproduce changes in tyre behaviour across different operating conditions instead of relying on a simplified constant-grip assumption.

After completing the vehicle parameterisation, I created the virtual track environment. The circuit was modelled considering not only the driving path, but also track elevation, road-surface friction and relevant environmental conditions. This was necessary to ensure that the virtual vehicle was being evaluated under conditions representative of the real test environment, as variations in surface grip and elevation can have a significant influence on braking, cornering and acceleration performance.

The next stage was the validation and correlation process. Before using the simulator as a development tool, the physical car was tested and the resulting telemetry was compared against equivalent simulation runs. I analysed signals including longitudinal and lateral acceleration, vehicle speed, steering response, yaw behaviour, wheel speeds and suspension movement to determine whether the virtual model reproduced the dynamic behaviour of the real vehicle.
Rather than validating the model purely from the final lap time, I compared individual vehicle responses so that any disagreement could be traced back to a particular subsystem or group of parameters. If a discrepancy was identified, the relevant assumptions, parameters or subsystem model were reviewed and adjusted before repeating the simulation. This created an iterative process of physical testing, telemetry analysis, simulation comparison, model refinement and re-validation, progressively improving the correlation between the virtual and physical car.

Once the objective behaviour of the vehicle had been correlated against real telemetry, the model was also evaluated using Driver-in-the-Loop simulation. This allowed the complete car to be assessed under realistic combinations of steering, braking and throttle inputs, while also providing driver feedback on aspects such as turn-in response, balance, traction and braking behaviour. This final stage was used as an additional validation layer before the model was applied to setup development, component evaluation and lap-time simulation.
projects.result:
Once the digital twin had been validated and correlated against real vehicle telemetry, it evolved from a lap-time prediction tool into a comprehensive vehicle-development and performance analysis platform. The project provided E-Tech Racing with the capability to evaluate the complete vehicle virtually, investigate interactions between its different systems and assess potential developments before committing valuable resources to manufacturing or physical testing.

One of the first major applications was the development and validation of the vehicle's dynamic control systems, particularly traction control, torque vectoring and regenerative braking. By integrating these strategies into the full-vehicle model, we could evaluate their behaviour under representative acceleration, braking and cornering conditions. Through Model-in-the-Loop (MIL) testing, we analysed their influence on torque delivery, tyre utilisation, vehicle stability, energy recovery and overall performance. This allowed us to identify limitations, refine control strategies and evaluate their interactions with the rest of the vehicle before proceeding to physical testing.

The simulator subsequently became an essential tool for vehicle setup optimisation and component development. Suspension parameters, tyre operating conditions, aerodynamic configurations and vehicle balance could be modified independently or in combination, allowing us to understand their influence on both individual vehicle responses and overall lap time. Rather than relying solely on theoretical assumptions or subjective driver feedback, we established a KPI-driven decision-making process, using measurable indicators such as lap time, sector performance, lateral acceleration, tyre utilisation, vehicle balance and energy consumption to compare alternatives. Every proposed change could therefore be evaluated against a defined performance objective, providing a quantitative justification for engineering decisions.

Another important application was track-specific performance simulation. By introducing different circuit layouts into the virtual environment, we could investigate how the car would perform under the particular demands of each track. This included analysing braking zones, acceleration profiles, cornering behaviour, energy consumption and setup requirements, allowing us to identify potential performance limitations and prepare development priorities before arriving at an event.

The integration of Driver-in-the-Loop (DIL) simulation further expanded the capabilities of the platform. Drivers could interact directly with the virtual vehicle, familiarise themselves with different circuits and provide feedback on characteristics such as turn-in response, braking stability, traction and cornering balance. This introduced an additional link between objective simulation data and subjective vehicle behaviour, supporting both driver preparation and setup evaluation.

Ultimately, the project established a simulation-led, data-driven vehicle-development workflow within the team. Instead of evaluating components and systems in isolation, we could investigate their combined influence on the complete vehicle, quantify performance gains through defined KPIs and prioritise the most promising developments for physical validation.

More importantly, the simulator changed how we approached engineering decisions: from asking whether a modification should theoretically improve the car to measuring how much performance it could deliver, where that improvement would occur and whether it justified implementation.
projects.challenge:
When I joined E-Tech Racing, I realised that the team lacked a complete simulation tool capable of predicting the performance of the car as a whole. Development decisions were heavily dependent on engineering judgement, isolated calculations and physical testing, with no common environment in which the effect of a change could be translated directly into vehicle behaviour and ultimately lap time.

I saw this as an important opportunity. In a Formula Student environment, track time, manufacturing capacity, budget and personnel are all limited, meaning that physically producing and testing every potential modification is neither practical nor efficient. At the same time, changes to areas such as suspension, aerodynamics, mass distribution, powertrain parameters or vehicle setup do not act independently, making it difficult to understand their true effect on the complete car when each subsystem is considered separately.

From this, I identified the need for a full-vehicle performance simulation capability. My idea was to create a tool that would allow us to move beyond asking whether an individual component looked better in isolation and instead answer the question that matters most in motorsport: would this change actually make the car faster around a circuit?

The objective I set for the project was therefore to develop E-Tech Racing's first full-vehicle lap-time simulation platform, creating a virtual representation of the car that could support the evaluation of potential developments before committing limited resources to manufacturing and track testing.
I also saw the potential for the same environment to support track-specific preparation and driver familiarisation, giving the team a better understanding of how the car was expected to behave across different circuits and operating conditions.
Ultimately, the project came from identifying a gap in the team's development process: there was no tool capable of connecting engineering decisions, complete-vehicle behaviour and lap time. My objective was to create that capability.

projects.title: Trackside Performance, Telemetry & Testing
projects.summary: Bringing data analysis to events and vehicle testing.
projects.approach:
My responsibilities covered test planning, circuit design, trackside telemetry, data acquisition and post-test analysis, working closely with the different departments to ensure that each session addressed specific engineering objectives.

Before each test day, I coordinated with the technical departments to establish their data requirements, define the tests to be performed and organise the necessary personnel and equipment. I designed dedicated test-track layouts using Google Earth and KML files, adapting the circuit geometry to the intended development objectives. Tight corners and low-speed sections were used for evaluating traction, torque vectoring and mechanical grip, while faster corners and longer sections allowed us to investigate high-speed vehicle balance, aerodynamic behaviour and dynamic stability. These layouts were then physically recreated using cones at our testing facility.

In parallel, we developed a basic wireless telemetry system, using an antenna-based communication link to receive selected vehicle signals in real time. This allowed us to monitor parameters such as suspension movement and battery-related information from trackside, with particular emphasis on estimating remaining energy and managing consumption throughout endurance runs.

Based on the available telemetry, we could assess whether the driver should prioritise energy conservation or whether sufficient energy remained to sustain a more aggressive pace. Where direct radio communication was restricted, this information could be conveyed through predefined visual signals.

Following each session, I was responsible for collecting and processing the recorded telemetry, reviewing the vehicle's response and identifying relevant findings. I then distributed the results to the appropriate departments, allowing suspension, aerodynamics, controls and powertrain developments to be evaluated using real testing data. This created a continuous feedback loop between engineering development, physical testing, data analysis and subsequent vehicle improvements.
projects.result:
The implementation of this workflow allowed us to approach physical testing in a more structured and data-driven way. Rather than simply running the car and collecting information afterwards, each session was designed around specific technical questions, ensuring that limited track time was used to investigate particular performance characteristics and development priorities.

The introduction of live telemetry provided additional visibility into the car's condition during running, particularly for battery-energy management. Combined with the recorded telemetry, this supported decisions about vehicle operation and provided valuable information for evaluating control strategies, suspension behaviour, vehicle balance and other performance-related developments.

My responsibilities also extended to trackside engineering during Formula Student Germany, Formula Student Spain and Formula Student Alpe Adria. Alongside telemetry analysis and performance support during dynamic events, I participated in technical inspections, vehicle preparation, troubleshooting and maintenance. I regularly worked beyond my own department, helping with the assembly and disassembly of suspension components, steering systems, wheels, aerodynamic elements and braking systems, including brake bleeding and component replacement.

These experiences gave me a much broader understanding of the relationship between vehicle performance, mechanical reliability, engineering preparation and trackside operations. More importantly, they reinforced the importance of being able to move between data analysis and hands-on mechanical work, contributing wherever necessary to keep the car operational and make the most of every opportunity on track.
projects.challenge:
Throughout my time at E-Tech Racing, I identified the importance of connecting our engineering development with the actual behaviour of the car on track. While simulation and theoretical analysis provided valuable information, physical testing was essential to validate our developments, identify performance limitations and understand how the different vehicle systems behaved under real operating conditions.

One of the main challenges was the limited availability of track time and the lack of a practical system for monitoring vehicle behaviour remotely. I therefore wanted to establish a more structured testing and trackside performance workflow, allowing us to maximise the engineering value of each test session while improving communication between the driver, the engineering team and the different technical departments.

A particular priority was energy management during endurance events. Without access to live vehicle data, assessing the remaining battery energy and determining whether the driver could increase pace or needed to conserve energy was significantly more difficult. The objective was to introduce a basic real-time telemetry capability that would support informed decisions while the car was running.

projects.title: Car Development & Setup Optimisation
projects.summary: Developing suspension geometry, transmission ratios and vehicle setup through full-vehicle simulation and performance analysis.
projects.approach:
The new suspension geometry and chassis parameters were introduced into the existing vehicle model using MATLAB, Simulink, Simscape and IPG CarMaker. The suspension was parameterised so that changes in geometry could be evaluated within the context of the complete vehicle rather than analysing the suspension independently.
Different design iterations could then be simulated under identical conditions and compared using objective performance indicators. This allowed us to study how changes to the suspension influenced characteristics such as wheel behaviour, load transfer, vehicle balance, lateral performance and overall lap-time response, while also identifying potential interactions with the tyres, aerodynamics and the rest of the vehicle.
This created a virtual development loop in which proposed components or geometries could be assessed, compared and refined before manufacturing. Instead of producing several physical versions and determining their effectiveness through track testing, simulation was used to narrow the design space and prioritise the most promising solutions for physical implementation.
Once the vehicle architecture had been established, the same model was used for setup optimisation. Suspension parameters, tyre conditions and vehicle balance could be modified and evaluated across different virtual circuits. Rather than looking only at total lap time, the analysis considered where performance was gained or lost around the lap and how the setup influenced the dynamic behaviour of the car.
Driver feedback was also considered alongside the simulation results. Where different drivers preferred different vehicle characteristics, the setup could be adjusted while still using objective data to understand the performance consequences of those changes. This allowed us to develop circuit-specific and driver-specific setup directions rather than relying on a single compromise configuration.
projects.result:
The project allowed several important vehicle-development decisions to be made before the corresponding components were physically manufactured or tested.
For the new transmission, lap-time simulation provided a direct method of comparing alternative ratios and identifying the configuration that offered the most appropriate compromise between acceleration, available wheel torque and maximum useful speed for the vehicle's expected operating conditions. Instead of defining the gearing from a single design target, the decision could be justified according to its effect on complete-vehicle performance around a circuit.
The same simulation-led approach supported the development of the new suspension and chassis, allowing multiple geometries and configurations to be screened virtually before selecting the most promising solutions for implementation.
Finally, the project established a repeatable setup-development workflow. Different configurations could be prepared for specific circuit characteristics and driver requirements, with every change assessed through objective KPIs before being validated physically.
Overall, the project connected powertrain definition, suspension design, setup development and lap-time simulation within the same performance environment, allowing major vehicle decisions to be made based on their measurable effect on the complete car rather than on individual subsystem performance alone.
projects.challenge:
The development of a new vehicle introduced several decisions that had to be made before extensive physical testing was possible. One of the most important was defining the gear ratio of the new transmission, as the selected ratio directly influenced wheel torque, acceleration capability, maximum speed and the operating range of the powertrain around a lap.
Rather than selecting the ratio from a single acceleration calculation or theoretical top-speed target, the objective was to evaluate different transmission configurations within the complete vehicle and circuit environment. This allowed us to understand the compromise between stronger acceleration from shorter gearing and the higher speed capability provided by longer gearing, and ultimately determine which configuration produced the best overall performance.
The same approach was applied to the development of the new suspension geometry and chassis configuration. Different design alternatives could be evaluated virtually before manufacturing, reducing the need for costly physical iterations.
Finally, the project aimed to establish a structured setup optimisation process, adapting the vehicle to the characteristics of different circuits and, where necessary, to the preferences and driving characteristics of individual drivers.

The project combined transmission ratio selection, suspension and chassis development, and setup optimisation, using lap-time simulation and vehicle-dynamics analysis to compare different configurations quantitatively and identify the solutions offering the greatest overall performance potential.

projects.title: 2026 F1 Active Aero Front Wing Concept
projects.summary: An independent active front-wing concept for the 2026 Formula 1 framework, combining CAD, mechanism design and CFD analysis.
projects.challenge:
The introduction of active aerodynamics for the 2026 Formula 1 regulations created a completely different front-wing design problem. The wing could no longer be considered purely as a fixed aerodynamic surface: its geometry had to satisfy the regulatory volume while also operating effectively in two distinct aerodynamic states.
I set myself the challenge of developing a complete 2026-compliant active front-wing concept from the regulations available at the time. The primary objective was to maximise useful front-end aerodynamic performance in the cornering configuration while creating a second configuration capable of significantly reducing drag on the straights.
This required considering not only the aerodynamic surfaces themselves, but also the kinematics and mechanical integration of the movable elements. The flap movement, rotation axis, achievable angle range and actuation concept all had to be incorporated without violating the prescribed geometric constraints.
The project therefore became an exercise in translating a technical regulation into a complete engineering concept, connecting regulatory interpretation, aerodynamic design and mechanical system development.
projects.approach:
The project began with a detailed review of the available 2026 Formula 1 technical regulations, using the prescribed bodywork volumes and bounding-box constraints to establish the allowable geometry of the front wing. The overall dimensions, element positioning and movable surfaces were developed within this regulatory envelope rather than designing the aerodynamic shape independently and adapting it afterwards.
From this initial geometry, I developed the wing surfaces and investigated different profiles, element relationships and angles of attack. The aim was to produce a configuration capable of generating strong front-end load in the normal cornering state while maintaining a controllable aerodynamic response across the intended operating range.
The active system was then developed around the movable flap architecture. I designed the kinematic movement and actuation mechanism, defining how the wing would transition between its cornering configuration and the low-drag X-Mode configuration. This included studying the rotation of the active elements, their required travel and the mechanical arrangement necessary to produce repeatable movement while remaining compatible with the wing structure.
The aerodynamic development was evaluated using CFD, comparing the behaviour of the wing across the different configurations. Pressure distribution, airflow structures, downforce and drag were analysed to understand how changes to flap angle and geometry influenced the aerodynamic performance of the assembly. Rather than seeking maximum downforce in isolation, the design process focused on the compromise between cornering load and aerodynamic efficiency, while ensuring that the low-drag configuration produced a meaningful reduction in resistance.
The project was completed with detailed CAD modelling and technical drawings, defining the geometry and mechanical interfaces of the final concept and converting the aerodynamic study into a fully documented engineering design.
projects.result:
The final outcome was a complete conceptual design for a 2026-style active Formula 1 front wing, developed from regulatory constraints through to aerodynamic and mechanical definition.
The project produced both a high-downforce cornering configuration and an active low-drag configuration, allowing the aerodynamic consequences of changing the flap position to be investigated within the same wing architecture. CFD analysis provided a quantitative basis for comparing the configurations and refining the relationship between wing geometry, angle of attack, downforce generation and drag.
Beyond the aerodynamic surfaces, the project also resulted in a complete concept for the movement and actuation of the active elements, together with the associated CAD models and engineering drawings. This meant that the project extended beyond aerodynamic styling into the integration of a functioning mechanical system.
Most importantly, it gave me the opportunity to work independently through the complete development process: interpreting a new technical regulation, defining the design space, generating an aerodynamic concept, analysing it numerically, developing the active mechanism and documenting the final solution.

projects.overview:
In 2025, following the publication of the new Formula 1 technical framework for 2026, I independently developed a regulation-driven active front-wing concept to explore how the new movable aerodynamic architecture could be implemented before the new generation of cars had entered competition.
The project covered the complete development process, from interpreting the regulatory geometry and defining the aerodynamic surfaces to designing the wing's actuation mechanism, movement range and technical drawings. CFD analysis was then used to investigate the aerodynamic behaviour of the concept in both its high-downforce and low-drag configurations.

projects.title: From robot to production
projects.summary: Industrialising a robotic MAG welding cell at Montesa Honda.
projects.approach:
I followed the complete industrialisation process from initial concept to series production. The project began with a technical and economic feasibility study, including investment analysis, capacity requirements and comparison of different cell configurations. I then benchmarked several suppliers and evaluated their proposals based on technical performance, cost, quality, delivery, maintainability and integration requirements before selecting the final solution.
During industrialisation, I coordinated the installation of the cell, adapted the existing welding fixtures and worked on the robot trajectories and MAG process parameters. The initial offline programs were progressively refined on the physical cell, optimising torch accessibility, welding sequence, non-productive movements and heat distribution.
Validation was performed iteratively rather than treating the first programmed solution as final. Weld quality was assessed through visual inspection and macrographic analysis, while 3D dimensional measurements were used to identify deformation produced during welding. When deviations were detected, parameters, fixture conditions and weld sequencing were modified and the parts were revalidated. Finally, the cell was integrated with the factory MES system for production monitoring and traceability.
projects.result:
The project resulted in a fully industrialised robotic cell operating in series production. For the Engine Guard, process and trajectory optimisation reduced cycle time by 25 seconds per part. A second component, previously welded manually in two separate stages, was redesigned around the new process and consolidated into a single robotic welding operation.

The final welding processes passed the required visual, macrographic and dimensional quality controls, while the cell reached approximately 92% OEE, exceeding the original 90% target. Integration with MES also introduced continuous production monitoring and traceability, while the flexible cell architecture left capacity available for the future introduction of additional references.

This project was also developed as my Bachelor’s Thesis in Mechanical Engineering, for which I was awarded 10/10 with Highest Honours for the thesis.
projects.challenge:
The project originated from the need to modernise the welding area at Montesa Honda, where ageing robotic equipment and manually welded components were creating limitations in reliability, repeatability and productivity. My objective was to develop and industrialise a new robotic MAG welding cell capable of manufacturing multiple references while improving process consistency, reducing cycle time and providing greater production traceability.
The scope went beyond the robot itself: the project had to demonstrate technical and economic feasibility, integrate the new equipment into the existing production environment, satisfy safety and quality requirements and achieve an OEE above 90% once operating under stable production conditions.

projects.title: Electric Motorcycle Conversion & Vehicle Integration
projects.summary: Converting a 1983 motorcycle to electric power, from restoration to powertrain integration.
projects.approach:
I began by completely disassembling the motorcycle and evaluating which original components could be restored and reused. The chassis, swingarm, bodywork and several mechanical components were refurbished before the vehicle was rebuilt around the new electric architecture.     

Different powertrain configurations were analysed before selecting an 8 kW hub motor, a programmable 72 V Sabvoton controller and a 72 V, 40 Ah battery with BMS. Component selection considered power requirements, mass, physical dimensions, reliability and compatibility with the original chassis. I also calculated the expected vehicle mass, power-to-weight ratio, battery capacity, theoretical range and charging time before integrating the system.   

Mechanical integration required measuring and adapting the suspension, wheels and hydraulic braking system, comparing mounting dimensions, axle diameters and component geometry to maintain correct alignment and minimise unwanted clearances. Problems encountered during assembly were solved iteratively, including developing a mechanical solution to prevent the hub-motor axle from rotating under torque.   

I also programmed the controller with a battery-protection strategy, progressive power delivery and three selectable driving maps ( Eco, Normal and Sport ) to modify the motorcycle's response depending on efficiency and performance requirements.     

Finally, I designed a custom fibreglass enclosure/fairing around the central section of the motorcycle. Its purpose was not only aesthetic: it provided a dedicated cover for the battery and electrical components, protecting them from rain and external exposure while allowing the new electric architecture to be integrated cleanly into the original motorcycle design.
projects.result:
The project resulted in the transformation of a 1983 motorcycle platform into a modern electric-vehicle architecture while retaining much of the original chassis and character.

The final configuration combined an 8 kW electric hub motor, programmable controller and 72 V battery, with an estimated vehicle mass of approximately 109 kg, a calculated power-to-weight ratio of 10.02 kg/CV, 2.88 kWh of battery capacity and approximately 80 km of theoretical range.    

Beyond the physical conversion, the project gave me practical experience in vehicle integration, electric powertrains, mechanical packaging, braking and suspension compatibility, electrical architecture and programmable vehicle controls. The different motor maps and power-delivery strategy also allowed the behaviour of the motorcycle to be modified according to the intended operating condition.

What makes the project particularly significant to me is that I began it independently at only 16 years old, long before starting my engineering degree. It was one of my first experiences taking a complex mechanical system, breaking it down into individual engineering problems and then designing, building and troubleshooting a complete solution myself.
projects.challenge:
I started this personal project at the age of 16, with two objectives in mind. The first was to restore a neglected 1983 Derbi Sport Copa 75cc and transform it into a fully electric motorcycle while preserving as much of its original character as possible.

The second objective was more personal. At that age, I was still several years away from beginning my engineering degree, but I already knew that I wanted to pursue engineering and work with vehicles. Since I could not yet gain experience through university or professional engineering roles, I decided to create my own opportunity and take on a project that would force me to approach problems in a more structured and technical way.

The conversion therefore became much more than a restoration. It gave me the opportunity to start working with component selection, mechanical design, vehicle packaging, electric powertrains, electrical integration, control systems and practical problem-solving long before beginning formal engineering education.
From a technical perspective, the challenge was to redesign the motorcycle around a completely different propulsion architecture. The motor, battery, controller, suspension, braking system and electrical components all had to be selected and integrated while considering compatibility, weight, packaging, safety and overall vehicle functionality.     

Ultimately, the project was my first attempt to move beyond simply being interested in engineering and begin actually working through an engineering problem from concept to a physical solution. That same motivation , to understand how vehicles work by designing, building and testing them myself was one of the reasons I later chose to pursue Mechanical Engineering.
